Chapter 4: The Garments and the Gift of Acceptance
You know, clothing’s one of those things that can mean so much more than we realize. Sometimes it’s about pride, sometimes it’s just about fitting in, and other times, it’s like a shield we use to protect ourselves from the world.
Think back to the day of the crucifixion—when the soldiers took Jesus’s garments and divided them up. They even cast lots for his robe. It might seem like just another detail lost in the chaos, but there’s actually something powerful hidden in that moment—a message about acceptance and what it means to truly belong.
Picture someone who’s always felt exposed, maybe even out of place. Losing your clothes in public isn’t just uncomfortable—it’s a loss of dignity. It’s being seen at your most vulnerable, with nothing left to hide behind. But here’s the surprising part: even in that place of exposure, there’s a gift. When everything’s been stripped away, you’re invited to experience real acceptance.
Most of us spend so much energy trying to cover up our flaws—trying to show the world a version of ourselves we hope will be accepted. But this story about the garments? It’s a reminder that true acceptance doesn’t come from what you wear or how you appear. It comes from being fully known—and still, deeply loved.
The cross is where every pretense falls away. What’s left is met with grace. The soldiers, without even realizing it, ended up showing us how easy it is to value the wrong things. While they were busy gambling for a piece of cloth, something far greater was being offered—a love that covers every shame, a grace that accepts every flaw.
And really, nothing—not even the loss of dignity or the exposure of weakness—can separate you from that love.
So if you’ve ever felt unworthy, or afraid of being truly seen, here’s something I want you to remember: acceptance isn’t about your appearance or what you’ve achieved. It’s a gift. Freely given, no strings attached.
The cross is where you can finally set down every mask, and let every wound be healed. That’s the real treasure—acceptance, just as you are.
